pinterest.title: German Wedding Traditions Explained: From the Polterabend to Sawing the Log
pinterest.description: German wedding customs run from a porcelain-smashing party a week before to a log sawn in half after the ceremony. See what each custom means, when it happens and which ones to keep, from the Polterabend and the veil dance to rings worn on the right hand. Customs vary by region, so treat them as a menu to choose from with your family rather than a checklist.

pinterest.title: What Happens at a Polterabend? The German Wedding Tradition of Broken Porcelain
pinterest.description: At a Polterabend, guests smash porcelain or stoneware, never glass, following the saying "Scherben bringen Glück": shards bring luck. The couple then sweep up the shards together. It is now usually held at least a week before the wedding, and formal invitations are traditionally not sent. Read how this German wedding tradition can work as a welcome party for a destination wedding.

pinterest.title: Getting Married in Germany: Why the Standesamt Comes Before German Wedding Traditions
pinterest.description: In Germany, only the declaration before the registrar at the Standesamt creates a legal marriage, so the civil ceremony comes first and a church or celebrant ceremony can follow as the celebration. Our guide to German wedding traditions explains what Australian couples should check, including the certificate of no impediment to marriage (Ehefähigkeitszeugnis). General information, not legal advice.

slides: German wedding traditions you did not know: from broken porcelain to a log sawn in half.
Polterabend: guests smash porcelain, never glass, for luck. Then the couple sweep up the shards together.
Saving cents for the bridal shoes: paying in small coins once showed a thrifty, steady wife. A statement about managing money, not a luck charm.
The Standesamt comes first: in Germany, only the declaration before the registrar creates a legal marriage.
Rings on the right hand: both partners in Germany wear their wedding rings on the right.
Baumstamm sägen: the couple saw through a log together. Push and pull in rhythm or the saw jams, which is the point.
Schleiertanz: the couple dance under the bride's veil, and whoever holds the biggest piece is said to marry next.

instagram_carousel.caption:
German wedding customs run from a porcelain-smashing party a week before to a log sawn in half after the ceremony.

At a Polterabend, guests smash porcelain or stoneware, never glass, following the folk saying "Scherben bringen Glück": shards bring luck. The couple sweep up together, because the clean-up is part of the custom.

After the ceremony comes Baumstamm sägen, where the couple cut a log in half with a two-handled saw. It stands for the co-operation a marriage needs. Games like this, and the Schleiertanz, largely take the place of speeches, so expect to be put to work.

For Australian couples marrying in Germany, the step most guides skip: the civil ceremony at the Standesamt is the legal marriage, so secure it first and build the celebration around it.

Customs vary by region, so treat them as a menu to choose from with your family rather than a checklist.

Which tradition would you keep? Tell us below, and if you would like help weaving them into your plans, a Wedded Advisor is happy to talk it through. Full guide via the link in our bio.
